captions.text: Welcome back to The Overpass.
Before we unpack what went wrong,
it's over to you.
Menti question one.
You may select more than one.
Which of these businesses do you think is responsible
for this incident?
Ironclad Steel Fabrication?
Meridian Construction Group?
Or Outback Heavy Haulage?
Well, that's interesting!
Jane will now display the NHVR's answers on screen.
So, let's unpack this,
stage by stage.
Stage one. Design and manufacture.
The NHVR's investigations reveal that Vince's fabrication drawings specified
the truss's structural geometry.
But Ironclad thought that tie-down and lifting points were
a site problem,
and something the transporter could sort out on the day.
Vince, was there any discussion with you about securing
the load? Do you have a record of that?
I mentioned it in passing during an Ironclad scoping
meeting. But as far as I know,
it never made it into an email or a
file note. So there is no record of my
comment, or the decision, anywhere.
Menti question two.
You may select more than one.
Whose job was it to ask,
how does this get transported and restrained,
before agreeing to the design and fabrication?
Aryav Nair, project manager at Meridian?
Rachel Whitfield, transport manager at Outback Haulage?
Or Vince Murphy,
design engineer at Ironclad?
Menti question three.
What should Ironclad have considered about the transportation task?
Loading and restraining of the truss during design?
The delivery timeframe?
The route? Or the hazards involved in the job?
Is the Load Restraint Guide relevant in a case like this?
Should attachment points for load restraint be considered in the design?
Is the absence of tie-down points concerning?
Should Meridian have considered the transportation task when ordering
the steel truss to be made?
Should Meridian have been responsible for developing a loading plan?
What parts of the transport task should Meridian have
considered? The route?
Time of day?
Hazards on route?
Or all of the above?
Meridian's project schedule was tight.
The truss fabrication was fast-tracked,
to meet the construction deadline.
Stage two. Engaging the transporter.
Meridian needed a transporter at short notice.
After consideration, Aryav went to Outback,
seeking a quote within a week.
Rachel, had your company ever transported anything like this
truss before? And did you,
or your company,
ask Ironclad for a loading plan?
Did you get one?
We've done some OSOM loads,
but this was the first time we'd done a
job like this.
No, we didn't ask for a load plan,
and one was never provided.
Aryav, had you used Outback Haulage before?
No. We intended to use Allgood Haulage,
but they cancelled at the last minute.
So we contacted several others.
Outback's quote was competitive,
and on the cheaper side,
so we gave them the job.
Hmmm. Well, Outback had not yet acquired the necessary
permits for parts of the journey,
and was operating under notice for the remainder.
Aryav, did you consider a journey plan,
or discuss it with Outback Haulage?
No. What's a journey plan?
Did you ask Outback if they'd carried irregular,
offset, and high centre-of-gravity loads?
No. We just knew they carried OSOM loads.
Mick, how long have you worked for Outback?
And do you have any experience with OSOM loads?
I started with Outback about 6 weeks before doing
the truss job.
I usually do general freight,
and a bit of livestock.
This was my first OSOM job.
I didn't even know what OSOM meant.
Rachel, why did you allocate the truss job to Mick?
Well, because I knew he was an experienced driver,
and he was available on the day.
Did you know if Mick had any OSOM experience?
Did you discuss it with him?
No, I didn't.
I just thought he knew what he was doing.
He's got a licence!
Okay. So, the rail crossing,
20 km before the school,
was a known hazard.
Outback drivers had discussed it after previous jobs.
But it was never recorded,
or written into a hazard register,
or handed over as part of a formal briefing.
It was not flagged to Mick,
by Rachel, or anyone at Outback.
Menti question four.
Should Ironclad have produced a loading plan?
Should Meridian have considered the journey plan as part
of the engagement process with Outback?
Should Meridian have verified Outback's capability to undertake this task?
Before engaging Outback Haulage,
should Meridian have asked them about the experience Outback
has with loads like this?
How they will restrain the truss?
And do they have any questions?
Does verbal confirmation count as due diligence?
Should Outback have considered formalising a journey plan and hazards?
Should Outback have asked questions about the nature of
the freight item,
and whether there was a loading plan?
When should they have asked those questions?
When first contacted?
Prior to picking up the truss?
Or prior to leaving Ironclad's depot with the truss?
Before giving the job to Mick,
should Rachel have considered whether he has the work
hours available? His experience with such loads?
His knowledge of load restraint?
And his knowledge of the route?
Stage three. The journey.
The rail crossing was a known hazard.
But a journey plan did not exist,
so there was nowhere to include it in information for Mick.
The afternoon before,
12 hours before the journey,
Ironclad loaded the truck.
Mick asked Ironclad if there was a loading plan.
He was told no,
and to use his judgement.
So Mick secured the 20-tonne load as best he
could, with all five of his load binders.
The next morning,
Mick didn't check the load or restraints before he left.
About 15 minutes from the destination,
Mick was surprised by the jolt as he crossed
the rail line,
but did not register it as the load shifting.
He hadn't been told about the crossing,
or any other hazards.
He drove past the Wattlebrook rest area.
Site access was considered,
but not for specific oversize loads.
And the load fell off.
Damaging the metal median barrier,
blocking the oncoming lane,
and striking the school bus as it swerved to avoid it.
Menti question five.
Whose duty is the route and risk assessment,
once it's already known from an earlier job?
Outback Haulage? Meridian? Or Ironclad?
When should the risk assessment have happened?
At the design stage?
The project planning stage?
Or when engaging Outback?
What hazards should have been planned for?
Load restraint failure?
Vehicles cutting in front of the truck?
The railway crossing hazard?
Or other hazards?
Should Ironclad have factored in supervising the loading,
and the load restraint,
before the truck left their depot?
Where does Meridian's duty end?
When the truck is loaded?
When the truck is on the road?
Or when the load is delivered?
Should Outback have assessed Mick's competency,
and provided him with any necessary training?
What training might be needed?
Type your answer into Menti.
With no loading plan,
what should Mick have done before departure?
Refuse the job?
Escalate? Or use his judgement and experience?
What should Mick have done when he felt the
jolt crossing the rail line,
15 minutes before the incident?
Stop at the Wattlebrook rest area to check the
load? Or keep going,
because he's nearly there?
And what action should Outback Haulage take following the
incident? Check on Mick's wellbeing?
Attend the scene?
Call their lawyer?
Or notify the NHVR
of a reportable incident?
Lots to think about.
To be continued,
in the next episode of The Overpass.
